records.claim: Over the last two centuries the dipole strength has been decreasing at a rate of about 6.3% per century.
records.passage: Over the last two centuries the dipole strength has been decreasing at a rate of about 6.3% per century.

records.claim: Measurements since Gauss in 1832 show a relative decay of about 10% over the last 150 years.
records.passage: The Earth's magnetic field strength was measured by Carl Friedrich Gauss in 1832 and has been repeatedly measured since then, showing a relative decay of about 10% over the last 150 years.

records.passage: There have been at least 183 reversals over the last 83 million years (thus on average once every ~450,000 years).

records.claim: The latest, the Brunhes–Matuyama reversal, occurred 780,000 years ago.
records.passage: The latest, the Brunhes–Matuyama reversal, occurred 780,000 years ago with widely varying estimates of how quickly it happened.

records.claim: Some sources estimate the four most recent reversals took on average 7,000 years.
records.passage: Some sources estimate that the four most recent reversals took on average 7,000 years to occur.

narration.text: Earth's magnetic field is already weakening.
Its main dipole has faded about 6.3% per century.
Fields have flipped 183 times in 83 million years.
The last flip was 780,000 years ago.
Now switch it off completely, for just one day.
Satellites and power grids would take more charged particles.
But the air wouldn't vanish in a day; that takes far longer.
So we'd survive, but our technology would feel it first.
